tagline: A heat-proof ant in a mirrored coat that forages at midday
summary: While almost everything else in the Sahara hides from the noon sun, the silver ant comes out. A coat of tiny triangular hairs reflects sunlight and radiates heat away, and it is the fastest ant ever measured, sprinting across scorching sand to scavenge before its own heat limit is reached.

stats.range: Sand seas of the Sahara, North Africa
stats.diet: Scavenges insects and other small animals, many killed by the heat
stats.conservation: Not assessed by the IUCN Red List

facts.title: A coat of tiny prisms
facts.text: The silver sheen comes from a dense array of hairs with a triangular cross-section. They reflect visible and near-infrared sunlight strongly, and also boost the ant's emission of mid-infrared radiation, letting it dump heat back into the sky even in full daylight.

facts.title: Five to ten degrees cooler
facts.text: The researchers estimated that the hair coat keeps the ants' bodies 5 to 10 °C cooler than they would be without it, helping them stay below their critical thermal maximum of 53.6 °C.

facts.title: Walking a thermal tightrope
facts.text: Foragers pour out of the nest in a burst lasting only minutes during the hottest part of the day. Below that window, predatory lizards are still active; above it, the ants themselves would die of heat.

facts.title: The fastest ant
facts.text: Filmed at midday, when the sand can reach 60 °C, silver ants ran at up to 855 mm per second — about 108 body lengths every second, the fastest speed recorded for any ant.

facts.title: Short legs, flickering feet
facts.text: Its legs are shorter than those of related desert ants. It makes up for this with stride frequencies above 40 per second, feet touching the ground for as little as 7 milliseconds, and leg swings of up to 1.4 m per second.

notes: Name: GBIF's backbone spells it Cataglyphis bombycinus (key 1319624, fuzzy match); the literature cited here (Shi 2015, Pfeffer 2019) uses bombycina, which is kept. No IUCN assessment found; conservation stated as not assessed. Wehner et al. 1992 (Nature) is paywalled: the 'thermal tightrope' fact follows its abstract (explosive midday outburst lasting a few minutes, thermal window bounded by predation and heat) as quoted in secondary sources; press coverage gives the emergence threshold as ~45–47 °C at ant height, not used as a number. The 53.6 °C critical thermal maximum and the 5–10 °C cooling figure are from the Columbia/Phys.org release on Shi et al. 2015 (CTmax originally from Gehring & Wehner 1995). Speed figures (855 mm/s, 108 body lengths/s, 60 °C sand) from the Company of Biologists release; stride/stance/leg-swing figures from the Pfeffer et al. abstract. Size: the paper's figures imply ~8 mm body length (855/108); stated loosely as under about 1 cm. Diet line ('many killed by the heat') reflects the scavenging habit described in Wehner's work and press coverage — treat as general. Images: wild ants photographed by the uploader in Erg Chebbi, Morocco (geotagged); the AntWeb specimen photo was rejected because its rubbed hairs don't show the silver coat.
